Foresaw
for-SAW
v. (saw beforehand; kept in view)
Greek proorao, to see before or in front of. At Acts 2:25 the sense is not prediction but keeping continually in view — Peter renders the Hebrew of Psalm 16:8, I have set the LORD always before me.

Biblical Definition

For David speaketh concerning him, I foresaw the Lord always before my face, for he is on my right hand, that I should not be moved. Peter is preaching at Pentecost, and the verse he quotes is doing something the casual reader may miss. Foresaw here does not mean predicted; it renders a Hebrew phrase about constant orientation. David wrote, I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved. To have God always before one's face is to keep him in view in every circumstance, and the consequence David draws is stability — he is not moved, because his attention is fixed on the One who cannot be. Peter then uses the psalm for a purpose David could not fully have known. The psalm goes on: thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption. Peter argues that David died and was buried and his sepulchre is with us to this day, so that the psalm cannot terminate on David — and concludes: he seeing this before spake of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not left in hell, neither his flesh did see corruption. Two kinds of foresight meet in the passage. David kept the Lord before his face, and in doing so was given to see beforehand the resurrection of the Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), under FORESEE: to see beforehand; to see or know an event before it happens; to have prescience of.

FORESEE, v.t. To see beforehand; to see or know an event before it happens; to have prescience of, or foreknowledge of.

FORESAW, pret. of foresee. Saw beforehand.

PRESCIENCE, n. Foreknowledge; knowledge of events before they take place.

PROPHECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come.

CORRUPTION, n. The act of corrupting, or state of being corrupt or putrid; decomposition of animal substances.

Key Scripture

Acts 2:25 — "For David speaketh concerning him, I foresaw the Lord always before my face, for he is on my right hand, that I should not be moved:"

Psalm 16:8 — "I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved."

Acts 2:27 — "Because thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption."

Acts 2:31 — "He seeing this before spake of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not left in hell, neither his flesh did see corruption."

Modern Corruption

Apostolic use of the Psalms is often dismissed as creative reapplication of texts that meant something else; Peter argues that the psalm cannot be exhausted by David and was spoken of the Christ.

expand to see more

The standard critical account holds that Psalm 16 is a song of personal confidence with no messianic reference, and that Peter has reapplied it in a way its author never intended. Peter anticipates the objection and answers it by argument rather than assertion: David died, was buried, and his sepulchre is with us unto this day, therefore the words thou wilt not suffer thine Holy One to see corruption cannot be true of David. The psalm makes a claim that David's own tomb falsifies, which means the psalm was always looking past him. That is not reapplication; it is the reading the text requires, and Paul makes the same argument at Antioch.

The related loss is practical rather than academic. Because foresaw sounds like prediction, the first clause is read as though David were forecasting, and its actual counsel disappears. David is describing a habit — the LORD kept always before his face, at his right hand — and the stability he claims is the fruit of it. A believer who wants what the psalm promises is being told how it comes: not by a settled temperament but by a settled attention. The man who keeps God in view is the man who is not moved, and Peter quotes the whole sentence because the confidence and the resurrection hope belong together.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek proorao (G4308), to see before; saleuo (G4531), to shake or move; Hebrew shavah (H7737), to set or place; mowt (H4131), to be moved.

expand to see more

Greek proorao (G4308) — to see beforehand, to keep in view; rendered foresaw and seeing this before.

Greek saleuo (G4531) — to shake, to agitate; rendered moved.

Hebrew shavah (H7737) — to set, to place; I have set the LORD always before me.

Hebrew mowt (H4131) — to totter, to be moved; what David says he shall not be.

Greek diaphthora (G1312) — corruption, decay; what the Holy One did not see.

Usage

"“I foresaw the Lord always before my face” — constant orientation, not prediction."

"“that I should not be moved” — the stability that follows the attention."

"“he seeing this before spake of the resurrection” — Peter's argument."
